lede: The same moments of 451 in Jordanes, the chronicles of Prosper and Hydatius, the Gallic chronicles, Gregory of Tours and the saints' lives. Each column shows the English; the reader carries the originals.

pairs.frage: The Catalaunian fields, near Metz, at Troyes, or five miles from Troyes at Mauriacus?
pairs.note: Jordanes joins two names the others keep apart and gives the field the size of a province. Hydatius, far away in Galicia, puts it 'not far from Metz'. The Gallic sources and Gregory name Mauriacus near Troyes; the Copenhagen continuation alone gives a distance. Modern proposals, from Châlons to Méry-sur-Seine and Moirey, start from these few lines.

Jordanes counts 165,000 and 15,000 more; Hydatius 'about 300,000', copied by Isidore; Prosper, the nearest in time, gives no number at all, and the Gallic chronicle speaks of countless corpses. The figures say how the battle was remembered, not how many fought.

pairs.frage: Trampled by his own men, speared by an Ostrogoth, or 'by whom, uncertain'?
pairs.note: Jordanes gives two versions and does not choose; the Gallic chronicle of 511 says it is unknown; Isidore makes him die as victor. The Copenhagen continuation and Gregory say only that he died, and Gregory gives the victory to Aetius, Thorismund and the prayers of Anianus.

pairs.frage: Reason of state, or the spoils?
pairs.note: In Jordanes Aetius fears that the Goths will overwhelm the Empire once the Huns are gone. In the Copenhagen continuation and in Gregory he sends Thorismund and the Franks home with a plausible warning and keeps the booty. The same advice, three motives.

pairs.frage: Neither side gave way, the Goths' valour, slaughter on both sides, a lion in its den.
pairs.note: Prosper defines victory by who went home; Cassiodorus, writing for a Gothic prince, gives it to the Goths; the Reichenau continuation and the Gallic chronicle of 452 record heavy losses on both sides. Jordanes' Attila, shut in his wagon fort, still frightens his victors.

pairs.titel: Orléans: before or after the walls fell?
pairs.frage: Fortified in time, relieved as the walls shook, or entered and then freed?
pairs.note: In Jordanes Aetius and Theoderic fortify Orléans before Attila arrives, because its Alan king might betray it. Gregory has the relief arrive as the walls are about to fall; the Life of Anianus has the Huns already inside; Sidonius writes of a breaking-in but no plundering.

pairs.frage: The Pope, the Huns' fear of Alaric's fate, famine and disease, or an army from the East?
pairs.note: Jordanes gives two reasons, Alaric's example (after Priscus) and Leo's embassy; Prosper, close to Leo, makes the Pope's presence decisive and blames Aetius for leaving the Alps open; Hydatius, far away, does not mention Leo at all; Cassiodorus has Leo sent by the emperor.

pairs.frage: A nosebleed on his wedding night, or a woman's knife?
pairs.note: Jordanes, following Priscus, insists on a death 'without any wound', and the funeral song denies treachery. Marcellinus, a century later in Constantinople, says a woman stabbed him and gives the haemorrhage as the other opinion; the Gallic chronicle of 511 says only that he 'is killed'. Prosper and Cassiodorus say he died at home.

pairs.frage: With Aetius in 454, with the 'last victory' of 451, or never, because the Germans saved it?
pairs.note: Marcellinus, writing under Justinian, says the Western realm fell with Aetius and has not risen since. Gibbon calls 451 'the last victory … in the name of the Western empire'; Creasy turns it into the victory that saved 'the Germanic element' of Europe. Sidonius in 456 counts Rome's twelve centuries running out.
